result:
The piano tuner arrived at nine, as arranged, and found the house already half-gone.

Not demolished — sold, or nearly. The furniture had been carried off in stages over the winter, and what remained was the sort of thing no one fights over: a hallway mirror with a chip in the corner, a coat hook shaped like a whale, the piano. The estate agent let him in. She was younger than her voice on the phone and kept glancing at her watch in a way that suggested she had somewhere to be but had been told to stay.

"It just needs to sound all right," she said. "For the viewings. People like to press a key."

He nodded. He had tuned pianos for forty-one years and had heard the job described many ways. *Just needs to sound all right* was one of the honest ones.

The instrument was an upright, black, German, older than the house. Someone had loved it, or at least dusted it. He opened the lid and the smell came up — felt and old wood and the faint metallic breath of strings that have been holding tension for a very long time. He set his case on the bench and took out the tuning lever, the mutes, the fork he no longer needed but carried anyway, the way a man carries a photograph.

The estate agent hovered. "Do you need anything?"

"Quiet," he said, and she laughed, and then realized he meant it, and went to stand in the kitchen with her phone.

He struck the A above middle C. It was flat, of course, and slightly sour in the way that told him the piano had not been touched in perhaps six years. Six years is a long time for a string. Things settle. The wood forgets what it was asked to do. He set the mute, found the pin, and began.

There is a moment in tuning — every tuner knows it, few describe it — when two strings that have been arguing stop. The beat between them slows, slows, and then simply isn't. You don't hear the agreement so much as the absence of the disagreement. It is like watching two people who have been talking over each other fall silent at the same instant and look at one another. He lived for that moment. He had built a life out of thousands of them, small and unwitnessed.

He worked up through the temperament octave. The house made its own noises around him: the tick of a radiator that no one had turned off, a floorboard in the room above shifting for no reason, the estate agent's low voice saying *Tuesday would be fine* to someone.

On the D above middle C he found the pencil marks.

They were inside the case, on the pale wood of the key frame where you would only see them with the fallboard removed. Small, neat, a child's hand growing less childish as the marks went on. *M — 5 yrs — Twinkle.* *M — 7 — Für Elise (first bit).* *M — 9 — Clementi.* *M — 12 — Chopin waltz, badly.* *M — 14 — Chopin waltz, less badly.* Then a gap. Then, in a different pen, an adult's: *M — 31 — came home, played the waltz. Still less badly.*

He looked at the marks for longer than he needed to. Then he put the fallboard back and continued.

He had children himself — grown, scattered, one of them a dentist in a city he had visited twice. Neither played. He had never minded that, not really, though he had once bought a small electric keyboard for a grandson and watched it become a shelf for stuffed animals. You cannot make people love the thing you love. You can only tune it and leave it in the room.

By eleven the piano was in tune, or as much in tune as a piano ever is, which is to say it was making a series of compromises that added up to something a person could sit down and play without flinching. He ran a few chords. The bass was thick and dark; the treble had that slightly glassy brightness that old Germans get. It was a good piano. It had been a good piano for a long time and would be for longer, if someone kept the room dry.

The estate agent came back in. "Finished?"

"It'll do for the viewings."

"Great." She was already reaching for the folder that meant payment. "Do you — sorry, this is a strange question — do you ever play them? After? Properly?"

He thought about it. "Sometimes."

"Would you? Just for a minute? I've been in this house eleven times and it's never made a sound."

He could have said no. He was not a performer, and his hands were tuning hands, not playing hands, thick at the knuckle. But he sat down on the bench, which creaked, and after a moment he played the opening of the Chopin waltz — the one everyone learns, the one in A minor, the one marked in pencil inside the case.

He played it badly. Not terribly, but badly, with the hesitation of someone who knew where the notes were but not quite when. He got through the first section and stopped, because that was as much as he knew.

The estate agent didn't say anything for a moment. Then she said, "That was nice," and it was clear she meant it and also had no idea why he had chosen that piece, and he did not tell her.

He packed his lever and his mutes and his unnecessary fork. At the door he paused and looked back at the piano sitting alone in the emptied room, black and patient, holding its new tension the way it had held the old.

"Tell whoever buys it," he said, "not to move it against the outside wall. And tell them there's writing inside. They should leave it."

She wrote that down. He was grateful, and somewhat surprised, that she wrote it down.

Then he went out to his car, and the house went back to being quiet, but it was a different quiet now — the kind that a room has after someone has spoken in it, and before anyone answers.
